opus-5.5.text:
I think the field has converged, in a fairly short time, on one idea: pair the generative power of large language models with formal verification. You let a model propose (conjectures, proof sketches, intermediate lemmas) and you let a proof assistant like Lean check every single step.

Why that combination? Mathematics is unusual among domains AI is trying to tackle because it has a perfect verifier available, at least in principle. In most areas, like writing, coding product features or giving medical advice, the reward signal is fuzzy. You need human raters or heuristics. In math, once a statement and its proof are formalized, the kernel either accepts it or it doesn't. There's no hallucination that survives a type checker. So the approach people have arrived at is to use that crisp signal as the backbone for training and for search.

I'd describe it as three layers working together.

The first is **autoformalization**: translating informal mathematics, the way humans write it in papers and textbooks, into formal language. This is the bottleneck. The amount of formalized math in the world is tiny compared to the amount of informal math, so whoever can reliably turn natural language into Lean unlocks a huge amount of data.

The second is **proving**: models that generate proofs, often with tree search or reinforcement learning, using the verifier as the reward. Systems that did well on olympiad problems showed this works remarkably well when the problem is well-posed and the search space is manageable.

The third, which I find the most exciting and which is still the least mature, is **conjecturing**, or discovery. Real mathematics isn't just solving given problems. It's deciding what's worth asking, finding the right definitions, building the intermediate structures. If AI is going to be a genuine collaborator for research mathematicians, it has to go beyond being a very good competition solver.

So the consensus approach is: informal reasoning for intuition and creativity, formal verification for trust, and a self-improving loop where verified outputs become new training data. The open questions are about scale and generality. Can you formalize enough of modern math, in fields like algebraic geometry or analysis, where the libraries are thin? Can you move from closed problems to open-ended research? That's where I think the next few years will be decided.

And I'd add one more point. I don't see this as only a math problem. If you can build a system that reasons rigorously and checks itself, that's a template for trustworthy AI reasoning in general, including verified software, hardware and science. Math is the cleanest proving ground for it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the field has converged on a fairly clear picture, even if people argue about the details.

The core idea is that math is the one domain where you can get a perfect verifier. In most areas, when a model produces an answer, you need a human or another model to judge whether it's right, and that judgment is noisy. In math, if you write the proof in a formal language like Lean, the compiler tells you, with certainty, whether every step checks out. That changes everything about how you can train. You can generate millions of candidate proofs, keep the ones that compile, and throw the rest away. The signal is clean. There's no reward hacking, because you can't fool the type checker.

So the recipe that most labs have landed on is some version of: a language model proposes, a formal system verifies, and reinforcement learning closes the loop. The model gets better at proposing because it's rewarded only for things that actually verify. AlphaProof was a very visible demonstration of this, and now almost everyone working seriously on the problem is doing some variant of it.

Where I think people still disagree is on two things. One is whether you need the formal layer at all. Some groups believe that if you just scale natural-language reasoning with enough RL on final answers, you get most of the benefit without paying the cost of formalization. And the cost is real. Writing math in Lean is painful, and the library of formalized mathematics is still a tiny fraction of what mathematicians actually know. My view is that informal reasoning gets you very far on competition problems, where there's a checkable final answer, but for research mathematics, where the object is a proof and not a number, you eventually need something that can certify correctness. Otherwise you're back to trusting the model.

The second disagreement is about what the goal is. A lot of the energy has gone into benchmarks, IMO problems, and that's been useful because it's measurable. But solving olympiad problems is not the same as doing mathematics. Research math is about choosing which questions to ask, building definitions that make a problem tractable, and working for months on something where you don't know if an answer exists. The current approach is very good at search, given a well-posed target. It's much less clear that it knows how to pose targets.

So my honest summary is that we've converged on the right engine, verified search with learning, and we're at the beginning of figuring out what to point it at. The infrastructure question, how to make formalization cheap enough that mathematicians actually use it, might end up mattering more than any single model advance.

astra-6.text:
I think the approach has converged on a loop between proposing mathematical ideas and checking them. A language model can suggest a proof strategy, break a problem into lemmas, or try different arguments. Then a formal proof system can verify whether those steps actually work. That gives you a much more precise feedback signal than whether an argument sounds convincing.

But there’s still a gap between proving a statement you’ve been given and doing mathematics more broadly. A lot of research is about finding the right definition, asking the right question, or realizing that two apparently unrelated problems share a structure. Those choices are harder to verify automatically.

So I’d distinguish convergence on a practical training approach from convergence on a complete picture of mathematical intelligence. Generating candidates, checking them, and learning from the results is a powerful foundation. The next question is how you use that foundation to discover mathematics that people actually find interesting.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the approach has converged on combining informal reasoning with formal verification. On the informal side, a model can explore ideas, suggest a lemma, or sketch a proof in natural language. On the formal side, you translate those steps into a language where a proof assistant can check whether they actually follow.

That gives you a useful feedback loop: propose a step, check it, and use the feedback to revise the argument. Mathematics is particularly well suited to that because correctness can be checked precisely once the statement and proof are formalized.

But verification and discovery are different challenges. Checking a proof doesn’t tell you which theorem is interesting, which definition will unlock a problem, or which direction is worth pursuing. So I see this approach as a strong foundation, while the bigger ambition is to make AI useful throughout mathematical research, including the exploratory work that happens before you know exactly what you want to prove.
